entries.title: Final rankings for the boys high school basketball Class of 2026
entries.summary: <p>When analyzing and evaluating the graduating senior class in Illinois, a narrative developed over the past couple of years: improvement.</p><p>The positive progress this group showed stood out as there were more Division I prospects — currently 24 and still counting — than originally anticipated.</p><p>At the top of the class, it can still be debated as to who the top prospect is in the state.</p><p>Here is the final look at the Class of 2026 in Illinois as they head off to join their respective college basketball programs this summer.</p><p><b>1. Jamison White, 6-8, East St. Louis</b></p><p>White made the most of his one year in Illinois, leading the Flyers to a 3A state title and to the top of the player rankings. He’s blessed with a strong, athletic frame while showcasing offensive tools, both in the post and facing the basket. Previously committed to Penn State, White will instead stay home and play at Saint Louis.</p><p><b>2. Lincoln Williams, 6-6, Kankakee</b></p><p>With size, length, athleticism and fluidity, Williams brings the physical attributes that stand out at the next level. Add in impressive production — the big wing averaged 24 points a game and became the Kays’ all-time leading scorer — and Williams is an enticing, high-upside prospect who remains uncommitted.</p><p><b>3. Mason Lockett, 6-5, Oswego East</b></p><p>Lockett is a potential jack-of-all-trades player with versatility at the next level. The DePaul recruit’s size on the perimeter and feel for the game is enough for him to continue ascending while his jumper gains dependability.</p><p><b>4. Marquis Clark, 6-1, Young</b></p><p>Following a November commitment to Tennessee, the tough, shifty Clark carried the Dolphins this season with huge numbers and monster games. The compact point guard will burst through an open seam in getting to the rim and has a lethal capacity for scoring the basketball.</p><p><b>5. Rashaun Porter, 6-7, DePaul Prep</b></p><p>The ultimate winner who checks off so many boxes when it comes to intangibles and impacting a game. An elite defender and tough rebounder, Porter was a huge recruiting win for Toledo.</p><p><b>6. Christopher Kirkpatrick, 6-3, New Trier</b></p><p>While an injury derailed his senior season, the Princeton recruit shined when healthy. Plays with an air of confidence. With step-back jumpers, solid footwork and smarts, he will hunt shots and is renowned for his comfort level in shooting the basketball from deep.</p><p><b>7. EJ Hazelett, 6-6, Kankakee</b></p><p>What you like about Hazelett are the ready-made skills as a scorer, combining both shooting range and physicality and touch around the basket. Headed to Indiana State.</p><p><b>8. Chris Bolte, 6-6, St. Ignatius</b></p><p>There is so much appeal when it comes to Bolte, who can play inside and out and impact the game in so many ways. The Yale recruit plays with all-out effort and a competitive spirit that can lift a team.</p><p><b>9. Rykan Woo, 5-11, DePaul Prep</b></p><p>The efficient scoring lead guard is still developing his point guard acumen, but he’s well schooled, intelligent and operates like he’s seen it all before. There is no doubting his ability to make a variety of shots — tough shots and in an efficient manner. Woo will play in the Ivy League at Brown.</p><p><b>10. Cooper Knowles, 6-9, West Hancock</b></p><p>Headed to Belmont, Knowles is a player who has always flown under the radar playing at a small school in the southwestern part of the state. Long, rangy, light on his feet and explosive off the floor, Knowles has a long way to go from a strength standpoint, but he’s just scratching the surface as a player.</p><p><b>11. Colin Stack, 7-1, Benet</b></p><p>While he may lack ideal post skills right now, Stack has soft finishing touch around the basket and face-up ability out to the three-point line. And when weight and strength are added, the potential is there to be a bonafide rim protector with his size and length. Stack has signed with North Dakota State.</p><p><b>12. Semaj Stampley, 6-1, Alton</b></p><p>A super offensive threat as a deadly shooter who connected on nearly 300 three-pointers in his career. Then he will surprise you with his more-than-you-think athleticism. South Dakota State landed a good one.</p><p><b>13. Jordan Williams, 6-5, Fremd</b></p><p>The Illinois State-bound Williams’ game is unassuming, but he’s a versatile wing who will stuff a stat sheet while providing high-level defense. Always engaged with an ideal demeanor and presence, Williams is all about doing what helps a team win.</p><p><b>14. Ben Okoro, 6-7, O’Fallon</b></p><p>The physical makeup is impressive. With his size and length as a run and jump athlete, Okoro’s ceiling is considerably high. While he needs to improve his perimeter shot, the Wisconsin-Milwaukee recruit uses his bounce off the floor and activity level to score at the rim and in transition.</p><p><b>15. Amir Danforth, 6-1, Rockford Auburn</b></p><p>What a career Danforth, who is headed to North Dakota State, put together. All he did was score 2,000-plus points and drain 300 three-pointers while emerging as one of the most lethal shooters in the state. He constantly puts pressure on opposing defenses with his quick release.<br></p>

entries.title: Obama Center releases grand opening weekend events schedule
entries.summary: <p>The Obama Presidential Center is preparing a big show for its grand opening next month.</p><p>The Center on Wednesday released its schedule of activities for its opening weekend on June 19-21. Many of the events are free, family-friendly and available to the public.</p><p>The activities in the 19-acre campus at 6001 S. Stony Island Ave. — ranging from live music, to dancing and face painting — may be the closest many people can get to being inside the Center's 225-foot museum tower for months to come. Tickets for opening weekend <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/06/obama-presidential-center-tickets-sales-demand-sold-out-june-july" target="_blank" >sold out in hours</a>, and reservations for Illinois Free Days (on Tuesdays) sold out past October.</p><p>Entertainment at the Center, under construction since 2021, will also feature "sports and play stations" at its Home Court athletic center. Expect to see mascots from the Chicago Bears, Blackhawks, Bulls, Cubs and White Sox, among others.</p><p>The museum debuts June 18 with an invitation-only grand opening ceremony, then opens to the public the next day — Juneteenth, on Friday, June 19. The public events will carry through that Sunday, which is Father's Day.</p><p>The idea behind the grand opening bash is to propel the center's mission to inspire and empower visitors.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/12/08/obama-presidential-center-home-court-building-opened-exclusive-look" target="_blank" >Obama Presidential Center’s first building is complete — Here’s an exclusive look</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/11/13/obama-presidential-center-jackson-park-delays-construction" target="_blank" >Obama Presidential Center takes shape after 10 years of delays and construction</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“These celebratory programs are only the beginning of the fun ways in which we will welcome visitors to campus. We will foster a spirit of civic engagement and joy," Valerie Jarrett, CEO of the Obama Foundation, said in a statement.</p><p>Other activities on opening weekend include:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-525996c0-59e2-11f1-b79b-81d176c0d80e"><li>Performances and programs featuring Obama Presidential Center commissioned artists;</li><li>Storytime and hands-on activities at the Center’s Chicago Public Library branch;</li><li>Double Dutch performances and hands-on crochet jump rope-making in Home Court;</li><li>Interactive experiences in the Fruit and Vegetable Garden centered on growing food and holistic well-being;</li><li>Talks in the Center’s auditorium;</li><li>Guided and self-guided audio tours of campus.</li></ul><p>The Center is planning for additional events after opening weekend, and throughout the summer:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-525996c1-59e2-11f1-b79b-81d176c0d80e"><li>In July and August, the Center will host a “You Are America” summer series of talks, films and community events for the nation's 250th anniversary. That series will kick off with a free Independence Day celebration called “The People’s Fourth,” featuring live music, self-guided tours and family-friendly activities.</li><li>Summer Garden Gatherings will be hosted in the Eleanor Roosevelt Fruit and Vegetable Garden every other week from July 12 to Sept. 20, in partnership with Urban Growers Collective.</li><li>On Aug. 4, an all-ages celebration of President Obama’s birthday will be held with a karaoke DJ set.</li><li>A 50-year-old-and-up walk-run club called At Your Pace will meet Thursday mornings from Aug. 6 to Oct. 8.</li></ul><p>Information about all Obama Presidential Center programming will be available on the Foundation’s website and event calendar and will be updated as programs are added. Check it out at <a class="Link" href="https://obama.org/" target="_blank" >Obama.org</a>.</p>

entries.title: Man fatally stabbed in Greater Grand Crossing over Memorial Day weekend
entries.summary: <p>Detectives are investigating the fatal stabbing of a 47-year-old man Monday morning in the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood. </p><p>His death occurred during the <a class="Link" href="2 dead, 38 wounded in Memorial Day weekend shootings in Chicago" target="_blank" >long Memorial Day holiday weekend,</a> in which 38 people were wounded in shootings and two people died after being shot, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/26/man-charged-in-death-of-2-year-old-boy-who-fatally-shot-himself-in-pullman" target="_blank" >including a toddler.</a></p><p>The still-unidentified 47-year-old man was attacked and found unresponsive inside an apartment in the 400 block of East 73rd Street, police said. </p><p>The man, who was pronounced dead on the scene, died of multiple sharp force injuries and his death was ruled a homicide, according to a Tuesday autopsy performed by the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Cubs analyst Jim Deshaies on the 'W' he had to have (take that, Nolan Ryan) 40 years ago this week
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a> TV analyst Jim Deshaies took a few minutes Tuesday to scroll through Baseball Reference’s “Today in Baseball History” page, something he’d done many times before. Mining for a nugget that might fit into that night’s broadcast is never a bad idea, especially when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/26/cubs-skid-reaches-10-as-pirates-score-early-and-often" target="_blank" >the team is bordering on unwatchable</a>.</p><p>He saw the name of Ty Cobb, who recorded his 1,000th extra-base hit on March 26, 1925, against the White Sox. And the name of Josh Gibson, who on that same date in 1946 homered for the Homestead Grays at Yankee Stadium. And that of Hank Aaron, who in 1969 swatted his 500th double to go with his 519 homers at the time.</p><p>Great stuff. What’s better than nerding out about baseball?</p><p>The 65-year-old southpaw scrolled on, and there it was:“1986 — Houston Astros pitcher Jim Deshaies records his first major league win.”</p><p>How about that?</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/26/cubs-skid-reaches-10-as-pirates-score-early-and-often" >Cubs’ skid reaches 10 as Pirates score early and often</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/24/cubs-astros-wrigley-field-chicago-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga-pete-crow-armstrong" target="_blank" >Cubs can’t stop losing — but other than that, everything’s fine</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It was 40 years to the day since Deshaies toed the rubber in St. Louis, struck out 10 Cardinals hitters — slugger Jack Clark three times — and got himself off the schneid in his fifth start of the season and the seventh of his career.</p><p>It’s safe to say the details of that game aren’t burned into Deshaies’ brain.</p><p>“Had I not seen it today and if someone would’ve asked me who my first win came against, I don’t think I would have known,” he said.</p><p>What he does remember, though, is the feeling he had early on as a rookie that his leash was short. He’d won a three-man battle for the Astros’ final rotation spot that had lasted all of spring training, and it was a team and a veteran rotation — with Nolan Ryan going strong at 39, and eventual 1986 Cy Young winner Mike Scott and Bob Knepper also in their 30s — built to win now.</p><p>“Nobody had said anything to me, but I felt pressure,” Deshaies said. “I hadn’t had a win yet, and it was Memorial Day. I didn’t know if I might get shipped out.”</p><p>In the last days of spring training in Kissimmee, Florida, Deshaies had braced for news — good or bad — from manager Hal Lanier. Instead, Lanier never got around to telling him he’d made the team. As Deshaies’ wife, Lori, prepared to hit the road from Kissimmee a day or two ahead of the team for wherever they’d be living, Deshaies told her, “Just head toward Houston.” If it was going to be the Triple-A Tucson (Arizona) Toros, she could simply keep barreling west on Interstate 10.</p><p>It turned out nicely that year for Deshaies, who won 12 games — at the time, the Astros’ rookie record — on a 96-win team that ran away with the National League West by 10 games only to be felled by the glory-bound Mets in the NLCS.</p><p>Deshaies was even more effective for the Astros in 1988 and especially in 1989, when he posted career bests in wins (15), ERA (2.91), innings (225⅔) and strikeouts (153). He later pitched for the Padres, Giants, Twins and Phillies and retired in 1995 with 84 wins in 257 appearances, 253 of them starts.</p><p>But his favorite start? That came in his rookie season, and it wasn’t his maiden “W” in St. Louis. It was in late September in Houston against the Dodgers, whom Deshaies mowed through in a two-hit shutout, striking out the first eight hitters he faced — at the time, a major league record — and 10 in all. It put him in double digits in wins and gave him a sense that maybe, just maybe, he was where he belonged even if he wasn’t as dominant as Scott or as awe-inspiring as the godlike Ryan.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/CBhHfwN9d0M?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Deshaies' eighth K in a row to start game"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“I was intimidated by Nolan, star-struck by Nolan,” Deshaies said. “He’d walk through the clubhouse and you’d just kind of watch him. It was an out-of-body, surreal-type experience.”</p><p>Exactly one night after Deshaies’ finest outing, Ryan started against the Giants and allowed one hit and no runs, blowing away 12 batters.</p><p>“After that one, I joked to Alan Ashby, our catcher, ‘You’d think he’d let me have the spotlight for once,’ ” Deshaies said. “But ‘Ash’ said, ‘You watch, Scott’s going to be even better tomorrow.’ ”</p><p>Anyone want to guess what Scott pulled off the next day?</p><p>Hint: It rhymes with “no quitter.”</p><p>And not only that, but Scott’s 13-strikeout no-no clinched the division title.</p><p>Jim De-who?</p><p>“Those guys were great,” Deshaies said.</p><p>Heck of a thing to be a part of for a 25-year-old just starting to find his way.</p><p>It all goes back to that first “W.” Deshaies is pretty sure he possesses a baseball from that game, though where it might be is another matter. He’s certain there was no beer shower in the clubhouse to celebrate his win, or anything else along the lines of what players do now. Lori was in Houston watching the game on TV. Deshaies is just about certain his older brother, Mike, wasn’t in the stands in St. Louis, because Mike went to a lot of his games and little bro always seemed to lose them.</p><p>Ah, well. So it wasn’t the biggest night of Deshaies’ life.</p><p>Forty years later, though, how nice to be able to look back on it.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-h/" target="_blank" >Mariah Woelfel</a></h5><p><b>Mayor in Rome</b>: Mayor Brandon Johnson has a meeting Thursday with the world's most famous Chicagoan: Pope Leo XIV. He will be the latest Illinoisan to meet the pope, who has given locals from his hometown, including Gov. JB Pritzker, private audiences since starting his papal ministry a year ago.</p><p><b>Papal plan</b>: Johnson plans to thank Pope Leo for his advocacy, which includes pushing back against the U.S. war in Iran, calling for peace in Gaza and criticizing President Donald Trump’s immigration policies. The meeting comes as Johnson attempts to shore up his political base before what's sure to be a tough reelection battle, though the mayor hasn't announced a bid yet.</p><p><b>The itinerary</b>: On Wednesday, a 50-member delegation will tour the town with members of Rome's City Council. Johnson is set to arrive Thursday and meet the pope at 3:30 p.m., when he plans to <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-k/" target="_blank" >present the pontiff with a jar of giardiniera</a>. Then Johnson will hold press conference at American University, and later has scheduled a fireside chat and dinner. On Friday, Johnson plans to tour a new Metro station and an affordable housing project with Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri.</p><p><a class="Link" >Here are the candidates for Chicago’s first-ever elected school board president</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-yd/" target="_blank" >Sarah Karp</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-yh/" target="_blank" >Emmanuel Camarillo</a></h5><p><b>In the running</b>: Tuesday was the petition filing deadline to enter the race for a seat on Chicago’s first fully elected school board. <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-yk/" target="_blank" >Fifty-one candidates are officially in the running</a>. All 20 district seats and the citywide president position will be up for grabs in the Nov. 3 election. Voters will get to cast a ballot for a school board member in their community and for the president.</p><p><b>Race for prez</b>: Five people are running for board president, a powerful position that holds sway over what the board debates and votes on. Four of them — Jessica Biggs, Jennifer Custer, former board member Sendhil Revuluri and attorney Victor Henderson — submitted petitions the first day and will face off in a lottery to get the top spot on the ballot. Hilario Dominguez, deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union and the CTU's preferred candidate, submitted his petition Tuesday.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: November’s election and the transition from a partially elected, partially appointed board marks the culmination of years of work by advocates. target="_blank" >Inside the making of a Second City show</a></h3><p></p><h5>By <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-tr/" target="_blank" >Mike Davis</a></h5><p>It’s a typical afternoon in April. Onstage at Second City, just after lunchtime, six actors are rehearsing a sketch for its newest show, "Pandemonium, Please Hold."</p><p>Being in the room for a Second City rehearsal is a stark contrast to traditional theater, whose rehearsals include a lot of dead air with actors standing around doing nothing as crew members problem-solve lighting, sound and technical issues.</p><p>But here, rehearsal is exciting. When director Carisa Barreca pauses a scene to give notes, the performers immediately start riffing. Ideas and jokes are flying in every direction. At one point, cast member Zoe McKee breaks out into song. It’s beautiful, but Barreca eventually reigns them in.</p><p>How do you problem-solve funny? How does Second City, a company known for being the training ground for sketch comedy legends, create skits that work? It all starts in the rehearsal room.</p><p>WBEZ got a behind-the-scenes look at the making of the now open show. You can <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-ty/" target="_blank" >read about it here</a>, or <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-tj/" target="_blank" >listen to the audio story here</a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-whjlytk-l-tt/" target="_blank" ><b>MORE HERE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>WBEZ reporter Mariah Woelfel and Sun-Times photojournalist Zubaer Khan are in Rome to cover Mayor Johnson's meeting with Pope Leo XIV. We're looking for your Rome recommendations to send them for their off-hours. Where should they go? What should they eat?</p><p>We want to know: What would you do in Rome? Tell us why.</p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Email your answer here</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story. Tell us your name and neighborhood so we can shout you out.</i></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE CHICAGO 📸</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b20000" name="image-b20000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c506714/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F5e%2F8d43a0f94eba8c5cf6bc0f9457ef%2Fozone-260527-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bbc6b26/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F5e%2F8d43a0f94eba8c5cf6bc0f9457ef%2Fozone-260527-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/62bad30/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F5e%2F8d43a0f94eba8c5cf6bc0f9457ef%2Fozone-260527-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A haze hangs over Chicago’s downtown area seen from the air near the 8700 block of South Jeffery Blvd, Tuesday, May 26, 2026. entries.title: Metra adding trains to Rock Island, Electric lines as part of new transit law requirement
entries.summary: <p>Metra is adding several daily train runs to its Rock Island District line starting June 1, the first step in schedule adjustments required by the Northern Illinois Transit Authority law that goes into effect the same day.</p><p>The commuter rail agency is adding four late-day daily train trips on weekdays and 18 more weekend train trips. The Rock Island line is also phasing out "flag stops," which require a customer to wave down a train for it to stop at a station, in favor of standard stops. Some stops have been dropped from the schedule due to low ridership.</p><p>The idea, Metra CEO Jim Derwinski said in a board meeting last week, is to move toward "regional rail service." Regional rail service means more frequent all-day trains, a shift away from the agency's 9-to-5 commuter schedule. The NITA law requires that Metra implement regional rail service pilots on the Rock Island and Metra Electric lines.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Under fire over tainted ‘Broadview 6’ case, Chicago’s top federal prosecutor outlines ‘sweeping’ reforms
entries.summary: <p>Chicago U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros announced<b> </b>“sweeping internal reforms”<b> </b>Wednesday<b> </b>to his office’s grand jury practices, in the wake of the “Broadview Six” scandal that has shaken the city’s federal courthouse.</p><p>Boutros also announced that he and the Justice Department had taken “swift action related to internal personnel matters,” though he didn’t share additional details. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >The “Broadview Six” case fell apart</a>, days before trial, after a judge discovered improprieties during grand jury proceedings. The alleged misconduct came to light only after a lengthy push by defense attorneys to get the judge to review unredacted transcripts of what occurred.</p><p>The allegations included a prosecutor improperly putting her personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges, a prosecutor having substantive contact with grand jurors outside the grand jury room, and a prosecutor excusing grand jurors who disagreed with the case.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/05/26/broadview-six-andrew-boutros-kat-abughazaleh-ice-trump-chicago" >Grand jurors in tainted ‘Broadview 6' case had contact with Chicago’s top federal prosecutor, defense says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Boutros’ office said in a press release Wednesday that the new process “will be more transparent, effective, and impactful while greatly reducing the likelihood of mistakes and errors.”<b> </b>It also said “many”<b> </b>of the reforms “are being implemented for the first time anywhere in the country.”</p><p>Still, the most specific reform identified by Boutros was “extensive, deep-dive training from national experts outside the office.” </p><p>That’s perhaps because of the secrecy that traditionally surrounds the grand jury process.</p><p>“These remediations should also be deeply curative and put to rest once and for all the divergent practices that have existed across the office for decades, including from one assistant U.S. attorney to another as well as from one generation to the next,” Boutros said. “That’s because these are clear, bright line rules that everyone must abide by, which should streamline and simplify the decision-making and disclosure process, as opposed to bedevil it.”</p><p>Boutros also acknowledged that, as part of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/22/broadview-six-federal-prosecutors-misconduct-tainted-cases-reviewed" target="_blank" >previously announced review</a> prompted by the “Broadview Six” case, defense attorneys in cases that might have been similarly tainted will receive transcripts — or “minutes” — from grand jury proceedings.</p><p>Charged in the “Broadview Six” case were former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian Straw, former Cook County Board candidate Catherine “Cat” Sharp, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael Rabbitt, musician Joselyn Walsh and onetime Abughazaleh campaign worker Andre Martin.</p><p>They were accused of joining a larger crowd that surrounded an immigration agent’s vehicle last September. The crowd pushed, scratched<b> </b>and<b> </b>otherwise damaged the agent’s SUV. Of that crowd, federal prosecutors charged only six people, all largely involved in local Democratic politics, raising questions about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/30/broadview-six-ice-trump-doj-justice-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >selective prosecution</a> and freedom of expression.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >Charges were dropped</a> against Sharp and Walsh in March. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >The remaining case was dismissed</a> last week after it was reduced to a misdemeanor matter.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" >‘Broadview Six’ charges dropped as Chicago’s top federal prosecutor admits case was tainted by misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Questions have since emerged about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/26/broadview-six-loretto-hosptial-ice-sheri-mecklenburg-andrew-boutros" target="_blank" >a separate prosecution</a>, involving former Loretto Hospital Chief Financial Officer Anosh<b> </b>Ahmed. Defense attorneys for a co-defendant of Ahmed’s are seeking permanent dismissal of the charges against their client, though no such motion has yet to be filed on behalf of Ahmed.</p><p>The former lead prosecutor in the "Broadview Six" case, Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg, also formerly handled the case against Ahmed. She left earlier this year to serve as counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee, though she's since been terminated from that role. Also involved in the "Broadview Six" prosecution were assistant U.S. attorneys William<b> </b>Hogan, Matthew<b> </b>Skiba<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andres<b> </b>Almendarez.</p><p>After the revelations in the "Broadview Six" case went public, Boutros sent an internal email to his office calling the three remaining prosecutors "courageous"<b> </b>for fighting "long and hard for a case they inherited when a colleague departed the office."</p>

entries.title: Family devastated after Tilden High honor roll student fatally shot while walking to school
entries.summary: <p>When Asucena Velazquez hugged her 17-year-old son before he left for school Tuesday morning, she never imagined he wouldn’t return home.</p><p>Pedro Ramirez was on his way from their Back of the Yards home to class at Tilden High School when he was fatally shot in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/26/17-year-old-boy-killed-2-critically-wounded-in-back-of-the-yards-shooting" target="_blank" >5000 block of South Throop Street</a>.</p><p>“It never crossed my mind that my boy would get hurt going to school,” Velazquez told the Sun-Times. “They robbed my son of his future,” Velazquez said.</p><p>Around 7:40 a.m. a stolen black Jeep Cherokee with four masked assailants inside stopped behind a southbound red minivan near 51st Street, according to a police report. At least two of them got out of the Jeep brandishing a "long gun," and "fired dozens of rifle rounds" in the minivan's direction.</p><p>The two men who were inside the red minivan, 55 and 61, were shot but were able to drive away and call 911 for help — but the two-sport Tilden athlete and honor roll student collapsed. </p><p>"During the barrage of gunfire, the victim, who was walking westbound on the south side of 51st Street was inadvertently struck one time in the right side," the report said. He was pronounced dead at 8:20 a.m. at Comer Children's Hospital. </p><p>Both men were take to Stroger Hospital. The 55-year-old man has since been released, while the 65-year-old is still hospitalized in stable condition.</p><p>A 911 caller who witnessed the attack gave police a description of the Jeep. Officers then chase it and took one of the four occupants of the Jeep into custody near 44th Street and Wolcott Avenue. The other three assailants got away on foot, according to the report. One pistol and one rifle were found in the Jeep. </p><p>Velazquez said she was at home when she got a call from the hospital that Pedro had been hurt in a shooting. When she arrived she said doctors told her Pedro died from his injuries.</p><p>Pedro’s death has left their family devastated, Velazquez said.</p><p>“He was a good boy,” said Velazquez. “He was respectful and caring. He didn’t mess with anyone.”</p><p>Velazquez said she wants justice for her son and hopes police will find those responsible.</p><p>A person of interest has been taken into custody, police said, but no charges had been filed as of Wednesday morning.</p><p>Pedro, who was born in Mexico and moved to the U.S. at 5 years old, was a junior at Tilden, where he played on both the soccer and volleyball teams.</p><p>His mother said he had dreams of going to college and studying engineering.</p><p>In the hours after his death, Velazquez said she’s received an overwhelming amount of support from Pedro’s friends and the community.</p><p>She said her son’s friends have stopped by and offered their condolences.</p><p>“His friends are destroyed,” Velazquez said. “I always knew he had a lot of friends, but I didn’t realize how much they loved him. But they’ve shown me that my son was an excellent friend and classmate. He was in the wrong place at the wrong time.'' </p><p>A GoFundMe to help Pedro’s family with funeral expenses can be found <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/apoyo-para-la-familia-de-pedrito?attribution_id=sl:a1a4eb96-1fef-4342-9cb1-5493dac673ca&lang=en_US&ts=1779838447&utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&utm_content=amp17_ta-amp20_t1&utm_medium=customer&utm_source=copy_link" target="_blank" >here</a>.</p>

entries.title: Estudiante de CPS regresa junto a su madre en Chicago tras ser liberado de detención migratoria
entries.summary: <p>Un estudiante de último año de la secundaria Mather, detenido por agentes federales junto a su madre en marzo, regresa a casa en Chicago.</p><p>Ricardo Navarrete, de 18 años, compareció en una audiencia de fianza ante la corte de inmigración el martes por la mañana y fue liberado de la custodia federal, según Kelli Fennell, abogada de la familia.</p><p>“Estamos felices de que esté de camino a casa para reunirse con su familia”, dijo Fennell en un comunicado enviado por correo electrónico.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los agentes de inmigración detuvieron a Ricardo y a su madre durante una comparecencia rutinaria en la corte por su caso de asilo en marzo. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/20/juez-ordena-la-liberacion-de-una-mama-de-cps-detenida-por-ice-su-hijo-adolescente-sigue-detenido" target="_blank" >La semana pasada, Liliana Navarrete fue una de las 18 personas liberadas</a> mediante una moción de hábeas corpus presentada ante un juez federal en Kentucky.</p><p>La lucha por su caso de inmigración continuará en las cortes de Chicago, han dicho sus abogados.</p><p>Ricardo y Liliana tenían una solicitud de asilo activa cuando fueron detenidos, y ninguno de los dos tiene antecedentes criminales, según los abogados de la familia. Madre e hijo llegaron a Chicago en 2022 como solicitantes de asilo provenientes de Colombia.</p><p>Su liberación marca una <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/21/comunidad-escolar-y-de-futbol-queda-conmocionada-tras-detencion-de-estudiante-y-su-mama-por-ice" target="_blank" >victoria para los amigos, familiares y otros que realizaron</a><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/21/comunidad-escolar-y-de-futbol-queda-conmocionada-tras-detencion-de-estudiante-y-su-mama-por-ice" target="_blank" >manifestaciones</a> y hablaron con varios medios de comunicación, esperando que la atención ayudara a traer de regreso a la madre y al hijo a Chicago.</p><p>Ricardo se perdió el baile de graduación de Mather la semana pasada, pero hay una posibilidad de que pueda regresar a tiempo para caminar sobre el escenario en su ceremonia de graduación el jueves.</p><p>El destacado jugador de fútbol se había comprometido a jugar para el prestigioso Truman College después de graduarse, pero esos planes han estado en el aire desde que él y su madre fueron detenidos.</p><p>Ricardo había descrito las difíciles condiciones en las instalaciones de detención a amigos y familiares, incluyendo haber sido mantenido en cuartos estrechos con docenas de hombres, haber pasado tiempo en confinamiento solitario y haber dormido en el suelo sin cobija.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
